meta.title: Who really said "People use statistics as a drunk uses a lamppost — for support rather than illumination"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not David Ogilvy. He used it about research in 1963; Quote Investigator traces the lamppost simile to A. E. Housman in 1903.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People use statistics as a drunk uses a lamppost — for support rather than illumination'?
meta.ogDescription: Ogilvy wrote a research version in 1963 without crediting anyone. The image goes back to A. E. Housman's 1903 Manilius preface.

answer.label: Not David Ogilvy — an older simile he borrowed
answer.authorDates: 1859–1936 · Latin professor & poet — earliest documented form, 1903
answer.sourceLine: David Ogilvy did use this simile, but not this way. In Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963) he wrote that marketing executives rely on research — not statistics — “as a drunkard uses a lamp post, for support rather than for illumination,” and he credited no one, because by then the saying had been in print for decades. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the image back to A. E. Housman’s 1903 preface to Manilius, where bad scholars “use MSS as drunkards use lamp-posts,” and finds the first close match of the statistics version in January 1937 — credited there to Andrew Lang, a credit QI calls problematic.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the popular wording matches no single documented source

source.heading: The closest David Ogilvy ever came

source.excerpt: You have actually got to use judgment. (I notice increasing reluctance on the part of marketing executives to use judgment; they are coming to rely too much on research, and they use it as a drunkard uses a lamp post, for support rather than for illumination.)
trail: 1903 — A. E. Housman, in the preface to his edition of Manilius, attacks critics “who use MSS as drunkards use lamp-posts,—not to light them on their way but to dissimulate their instability.” Quote Investigator calls this the earliest precursor, and hypothesises the family descends from it ↗.

January 1937 — Francis Yeats-Brown’s Lancer at Large supplies the first close match for the statistics version, with a footnote crediting “Andrew Lang’s agreeable analogy” — as QI transcribes it ↗. Reader’s Digest carries the Lang attribution that April, and the saying spreads through Parliament, textbooks and magazines the same year.

1963 — David Ogilvy uses the simile in Confessions of an Advertising Man, aimed at market research and without attribution ↗. The book went on to sell more than a million copies ↗, which is how his name got fixed to the line.

Still today — quotation dictionaries keep the Lang credit alive, sourced to a “1910 Speech” known only at second hand through Alan L. Mackay’s 1977 anthology ↗, while the internet reassigns it to Ogilvy, Twain and whoever else is handy.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from page 100 of the 1963 Atheneum edition. Note what it is not: the subject is market research rather than statistics, the phrasing is “a drunkard” and “a lamp post,” and Ogilvy names no source — the saying was already twenty-six years into print circulation when he used it.

author.name: A. E. Housman
author.heading: A. E. Housman
author.bio: Alfred Edward Housman was Kennedy Professor of Latin at Cambridge from 1911 until his death in 1936, and to the wider public the author of A Shropshire Lad. His scholarly prefaces are famous for their invective: between 1903 and 1930 he published a five-volume critical edition of the Roman poet Manilius’s Astronomicon, and used its opening preface to flay editors who cited manuscripts selectively. The drunkard-and-lamppost image is his sharpest line in that vein — aimed not at statisticians but at critics who lean on evidence instead of reading it.

misattribution.heading: Three claims, none of them clean
misattribution.intro: This is a saying that collects confident credits. Quote Investigator ↗ opens its investigation by listing the candidates outright: Andrew Lang, A. E. Housman, David Ogilvy, or nobody at all.

items.scope: The version posted on business slides
items.why: Ogilvy’s documented sentence, on page 100 of Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963), is about executives relying on research — “they use it as a drunkard uses a lamp post, for support rather than for illumination” — and he attributes it to no one. QI ↗ records the statistics version in print from January 1937, decades before his book.

items.scope: The credit in the standard reference books
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ traces the usual citation to a “1910 Speech” known only through Alan L. Mackay’s The Harvest of a Quiet Eye (1977). QI ↗ finds no direct evidence: the Lang credit first surfaces in 1937, twenty-five years after Lang died in 1912, and QI puts it down to imperfect memory.

“People use statistics as a drunk uses a lamppost” is a smoothed later form. The January 1937 text QI transcribes ↗ reads “use statistics as a drunken man uses lamp-posts, for support rather than for illumination.”

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: Housman can be credited with his own 1903 sentence, QI hypothesises the later statistics version evolved from it, the Lang ascription is problematic, and Ogilvy simply reached for a simile already in general circulation.

context.heading: Why Ogilvy's name stuck to it
lead: Ogilvy is a plausible-sounding culprit for a reason: he really did put the simile into a book that a great many business readers actually read. Confessions of an Advertising Man appeared in 1963 and, by Wikipedia’s account, sold more than a million copies ↗. A line encountered there, in a chapter about the misuse of research, is a line you remember as his.

But Ogilvy’s target was market research, not statistics, and he offered no attribution — the mark of a man repeating something already in the air. It was: Quote Investigator ↗ documents the statistics version circulating from January 1937, through Reader’s Digest that April, into Parliament, textbooks and newspaper columns long before 1963.
detailsBody: Housman’s 1903 sentence is about textual criticism, and it is nastier than any of its descendants. As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, he attacked “gentlemen who use MSS as drunkards use lamp-posts,—not to light them on their way but to dissimulate their instability.”

The modern saying keeps the drunkard and the lamppost but flips the second half from concealment to support, and swaps manuscripts for statistics. That is a family of expressions evolving in circulation, not one sentence being quoted — which is exactly why no single primary source produces the wording people post today.
context.pull: Ogilvy was quoting the room, not coining a line.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article on this saying lists Andrew Lang, A. E. Housman, David Ogilvy and Apocryphal/Anonymous as candidates; transcribes Housman's 1903 preface line ('gentlemen who use MSS as drunkards use lamp-posts,—not to light them on their way but to dissimulate their instability') from M. Manilii Astronomicon (Grant Richards, London); gives Francis Yeats-Brown's Lancer at Large (Viking Press, New York, January 1937) as the first close match, footnoted 'Andrew Lang's agreeable analogy'; records Reader's Digest April 1937, Parliament April 1937, Pelsma's textbook July 1937, Atlantic Monthly August 1937; transcribes David Ogilvy's 1963 sentence from Confessions of an Advertising Man (Atheneum, New York, p. 100); and concludes Housman originated the concept in 1903 while the Lang ascription, arriving 25 years after his 1912 death, is problematic and unsupported by direct evidence.

Wikiquote's Andrew Lang page carries 'Politicians use statistics in the same way that a drunk uses lamp-posts—for support rather than illumination' in the main Quotes section, sourced to a '1910 Speech, quoted in Alan L. Mackay The Harvest of a Quiet Eye (1977), as reported in Chambers Dictionary of Quotations (2005), p. 488', notes the variant wording, notes wide attribution to Lang in Oxford and Columbia quotation dictionaries, and gives Lang's dates as 31 March 1844 – 20 July 1912.

Wikipedia gives David Ogilvy's dates as 23 June 1911 – 21 July 1999, describes him as a British advertising tycoon and founder of Ogilvy & Mather (started 1949), and dates Confessions of an Advertising Man to 1963.

Wikipedia gives A. E. Housman's dates as 26 March 1859 – 30 April 1936, states he was Kennedy Professor of Latin at Cambridge from 1911 until his death, and states that between 1903 and 1930 he published his critical edition of Manilius's Astronomicon in five volumes.
Wikipedia's article on Confessions of an Advertising Man gives the author as David Ogilvy, first publication 1963, publisher Atheneum, and states the book 'sold more than one million copies'.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Confessions of an Advertising Man by David Ogilvy, Atheneum, 1963.

The Classical Review (Volume 18, Issue 1, February 1904) carries a notice of 'M. Manilii Astronomicon liber primus: recensuit et enarrauit A. E. Housman ... Londinii apud Grant Richards', confirming the Grant Richards edition of Housman's Manilius Book I.
